title: Track4D: Representing Dense 3D Tracking for Video Diffusion Models
claim: Dense tracking can be cast as conditional generation: a frozen-backbone adapted generator maps video and geometry to outputs that decode into tracks.
layout: 2 stacked panels, left-to-right flow, dashed boxes mark trainable parts, red residual skip arrow
description: Two stacked pipeline diagrams. Panel (a), Generative readout (RTV and NCMV): a video and point maps from a frozen 3D reconstructor feed a frozen VAE encoder. The encoder output goes to a central dashed Video DiT box labeled Wan + LoRA. Ground-truth RTV and NCMV, used in training only, enter as noisy targets. A VAE decoder then produces RTV and NCMV frame stacks. RTV is added to the query-frame point map via a red skip arrow, and NCMV passes through a frozen 2D tracker plus lifting. Both paths end at a colored dense 3D track point cloud. Panel (b), Regression readout (Track4D-Reg): a World expert and a Motion expert exchange joint attention, followed by a DPT readout and a residual sum. Red marks inputs, blue marks outputs, and snowflake and flame icons mark frozen and trained modules.
caption: TRACK4D overview. (a) Generative readout. A frozen reconstructor supplies point maps P; the video VAE encodes them with video V into condition C. The LoRA-adapted video DiT denoises the RTV and NCMV latents, jointly by default, and the VAE decodes the videos. Hatched targets are noised in training and start from Gaussian noise at inference. Adding inverse-normalized RTV offsets to the query-frame point map gives 3D tracks; NCMV requires 2D tracking and lifting. (b) Regression readout. Point maps enter through a patch encoder, a private motion expert attends jointly with the video DiT, and a DPT head reads residuals without the output VAE (Section 3.4 and Figure 8). Flames denote trained modules, snowflakes frozen modules.
abstract: We study how to repurpose video diffusion models (VDMs), pretrained on millions of videos, for dense 3D point tracking, where training data is scarce. Doing so is non-trivial, as it requires representing 3D tracks as video-like signals that may lie outside the natural-video distribution on which the VDM was trained. We thus systematically assess the effectiveness of two such video representations. The first, Residual 3D Tracking Video (RTV), encodes per-pixel 3D offsets relative to a query frame and allows recovery of 3D trajectories directly from the generated video. The second, Normalized Coordinate Map Video (NCMV), labels each pixel with a canonical coordinate invariant through time. This is closer to a natural video and easier for the VDM to learn, but requires additional post-processing with an off-the-shelf 2D tracker to recover 3D tracks. RTV tracks more accurately, while NCMV shows that a VDM can generate dense correspondence as a video. We instantiate both representations with LoRA adaptation of a frozen Wan backbone, conditioned on point maps from an off-the-shelf 3D reconstructor as a geometric scaffold. Trained with a single dynamic 3D tracking dataset, Track4D achieves competitive zero-shot tracking on four real and synthetic benchmarks. A regression readout that bypasses the video VAE and uses additional training data brings further improvement, demonstrating the potential of this direction for dense 3D tracking. We hope our analysis will inspire future work that leverages VDM priors for dense 3D tracking and 4D reconstruction. Project page: https://nirvanalan.github.io/projects/track4d
